name: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV)
tagline: Understanding HIV: Biology, Transmission, Testing, Prevention & Modern Care
summary: HIV is a virus that targets the body's immune system, specifically CD4 T cells. With modern Antiretroviral Therapy (ART), people living with HIV lead long, healthy, and fulfilling lives.
whatIsIt: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) is a retrovirus that infects cells of the human immune system, primarily CD4+ T helper lymphocytes. When left unmanaged, the gradual depletion of these cells weakens the immune defense. However, modern medical advances have transformed HIV into a manageable chronic health condition. With daily Antiretroviral Therapy (ART), the viral load can be suppressed to undetectable levels (Undetectable = Untransmittable or U=U), preventing disease progression and sexual transmission.
causes: HIV is caused by infection with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV-1 or HIV-2 strains). The virus replicates inside CD4 immune cells, slowly impairing the body's natural defense against other opportunistic infections.
howItSpreads: Unprotected sexual contact with a partner who has a detectable viral load
Sharing unsterilized needles, syringes, or injection drug equipment
From parent to infant during pregnancy, childbirth, or breastfeeding (substantially prevented with maternal ART)
Unscreened blood transfusions (rare in modern certified blood banks)
howItDoesNotSpread: Casual contact: shaking hands, hugging, closed-mouth kissing, or high-fives
Sharing food, utensils, drinking glasses, or water bottles
Mosquito bites or other insect bites
Sharing toilets, swimming pools, gym equipment, or bath towels
Coughing, sneezing, saliva, sweat, or tears
symptoms: Early stage (2-4 weeks after exposure): Mild flu-like symptoms, fever, sore throat, swollen lymph glands, fatigue, rash
Clinical latency (asymptomatic stage): May cause no symptoms for years while the virus replicates slowly
Advanced stage (without ART): Recurrent fevers, persistent weight loss, prolonged diarrhea, chronic night sweats, frequent infections
riskFactors: Unprotected sexual intercourse without pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP)
Having an untreated sexually transmitted infection (STI) which causes mucosal inflammation
Accidental needle-stick injuries in healthcare settings without post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP)
testing: Modern diagnostic tests are safe, confidential, and highly accurate: 4th generation Antigen/Antibody (Ag/Ab) blood tests, rapid point-of-care fingerstick tests, and HIV RNA viral load assays.
diagnosisOverview: Diagnosis requires confirmed positive laboratory testing (ELISA/CLIA followed by confirmatory supplemental assay). A CD4 count and viral load baseline are then established.
prevention: Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP): Highly effective daily or long-acting medication taken by HIV-negative individuals to prevent acquiring HIV
Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP): Emergency 28-day antiretroviral course started within 72 hours of potential exposure
Consistent condom usage during sexual encounters
Using sterile single-use needles and medical equipment
Regular confidential screening for individuals and couples
treatmentOverview: Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) consists of daily combinations of medications that block viral replication. When taken as prescribed, ART suppresses viral loads to undetectable levels, allowing the immune system to rebuild. Effective ART also eliminates sexual transmission risk (U=U: Undetectable = Untransmittable).
whenToSeekCare: Seek immediate consultation if you have had a potential exposure within the last 72 hours to initiate emergency PEP. Routine confidential testing is recommended as part of comprehensive adult wellness.

mythsAndFacts.fact: With prompt diagnosis and consistent daily ART, individuals with HIV have a life expectancy comparable to the general population.

mythsAndFacts.myth: You can catch HIV from sharing cups or toilet seats.
mythsAndFacts.fact: HIV cannot survive long outside the human body and is not transmitted through saliva, sweat, surfaces, or casual contact.

mythsAndFacts.myth: People with undetectable viral loads can transmit HIV.
mythsAndFacts.fact: Decades of global clinical trials prove that Undetectable equals Untransmittable (U=U).

faqs.question: What is the difference between HIV and AIDS?
faqs.answer: HIV is the virus itself. AIDS (Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome) is an advanced medical stage defined by severe CD4 cell loss or specific opportunistic illnesses. With modern treatment, the vast majority of people with HIV never develop AIDS.

faqs.question: Is HIV testing confidential at CareSphere?
faqs.answer: Yes. All diagnostic screenings and physician consultations adhere strictly to patient confidentiality and professional medical privacy standards.

name: Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS)
tagline: Clinical Stage Overview, Immune Preservation & Comprehensive Management
summary: AIDS is the advanced clinical stage of untreated HIV infection, characterized by marked immune depletion. Early detection and modern ART prevent progression to this stage.
whatIsIt: Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS) is not a separate virus; it is the most advanced clinical stage of prolonged, untreated HIV infection. It is diagnosed when a person's CD4 T-cell count drops below 200 cells per cubic millimeter of blood (normal range is 500-1,500) or when an individual develops one or more specific opportunistic infections or cancers (such as Pneumocystis pneumonia, esophageal candidiasis, or Kaposi's sarcoma). Today, with early testing and widespread access to Antiretroviral Therapy (ART), progression to AIDS is preventable and reversible with prompt clinical intervention.
causes: AIDS develops only as a consequence of long-standing, unmanaged HIV infection where the viral replication has systematically damaged the immune system over a span of several years.
howItSpreads: AIDS itself does not spread from person to person. The underlying virus (HIV) is transmitted via blood, genital fluids, or parent-to-child during birth/breastfeeding. Stigma-free education emphasizes that touching, breathing the same air, or living with someone cannot transmit the virus.
howItDoesNotSpread: Shaking hands, hugging, or social contact
Sharing utensils, towels, or bed linen
symptoms: Rapid, unexplained weight loss (wasting syndrome)
Recurring fever or profuse night sweats
Extreme and unexplained prolonged fatigue
Prolonged swelling of the lymph glands in the armpits, groin, or neck
Chronic diarrhea lasting for more than a week
Persistent sores in the mouth, anus, or genitals
Pneumonia and recurrent severe bacterial infections
riskFactors: Undiagnosed or untreated HIV infection over multiple years
Discontinuation or non-adherence to prescribed antiretroviral medications
testing: Testing includes CD4 lymphocyte enumeration, HIV RNA quantification, and targeted diagnostic cultures/imaging for opportunistic infections.
diagnosisOverview: Clinical diagnosis criteria: Confirmed HIV positive status accompanied by a CD4 count < 200 cells/mm³ or presentation of a defined AIDS-defining illness.
prevention: Early voluntary HIV testing and immediate initiation of ART upon diagnosis
Strict adherence to prescribed antiretroviral regimens
Prophylactic antimicrobial medications (e.g., Cotrimoxazole) for patients with low CD4 counts to prevent opportunistic infections
treatmentOverview: Treatment involves immediate ART initiation to suppress viral replication, combined with targeted therapies and antimicrobial prophylaxis for specific opportunistic conditions. Even at advanced stages, robust immune recovery is frequently achievable with consistent medical care.
whenToSeekCare: Seek urgent medical attention if experiencing unexplained persistent fevers, rapid weight loss, chronic breathing difficulty, or neurological symptoms.

mythsAndFacts.myth: An HIV diagnosis means you have AIDS.
mythsAndFacts.fact: No. HIV is the virus. AIDS only occurs if HIV remains untreated for many years. Most people diagnosed early and treated never develop AIDS.

mythsAndFacts.myth: Once you have an AIDS diagnosis, recovery is impossible.
mythsAndFacts.fact: With modern antiretroviral treatments and antimicrobial prophylaxis, CD4 counts can rebound above 200 and immune function can be substantially restored.

faqs.question: Can AIDS be prevented after HIV exposure?
faqs.answer: Yes. Consistent daily adherence to antiretroviral therapy keeps HIV suppressed and completely prevents progression to AIDS.

name: Dengue Fever
tagline: Vector-Borne Viral Infection: Warning Signs, Hydration & Care
summary: Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral illness common in tropical climates like Tamil Nadu. Key management focuses on hydration, temperature control, and platelet monitoring.
whatIsIt: Dengue is a viral infection transmitted to humans through the bites of infected female Aedes mosquitoes (predominantly Aedes aegypti). The virus has four distinct serotypes (DENV 1-4). While most episodes cause a sudden high fever and intense body aches ('breakbone fever'), vigilance for plasma leakage and platelet drops during the critical phase is essential.
causes: Infection with the Dengue virus transmitted through daytime-biting Aedes mosquitoes that breed in clean, stagnant water.
howItSpreads: Bite of an infected Aedes mosquito
Not spread directly from person to person through casual contact
symptoms: Sudden onset high fever (103°F - 105°F)
Severe retro-orbital (behind the eye) headache
Severe joint, bone, and muscle pains
Nausea, vomiting, and loss of appetite
Mild skin rash appearing 3-5 days after fever onset
riskFactors: Living in or traveling to tropical endemic areas during monsoon/post-monsoon seasons
Stagnant water containers in or around households
Secondary infection with a different dengue serotype increases risk of severe dengue
testing: Dengue NS1 Antigen (detectable in days 1-5), Dengue IgM/IgG antibody serology, Complete Blood Count (CBC) to track hematocrit and platelet counts.
diagnosisOverview: Clinical assessment combined with rapid NS1 antigen and daily serial CBC monitoring.
prevention: Eliminate stagnant water sources (flower pots, tyres, cooler trays)
Use mosquito repellents, window screens, and bed nets
Wear protective long-sleeved clothing during daytime hours
treatmentOverview: Supportive care is paramount: abundant oral rehydration salts (ORS), tender coconut water, adequate rest, and Paracetamol for fever. Avoid NSAIDs (such as Ibuprofen or Aspirin) as they may increase bleeding risks. Hospitalization is required if warning signs appear.
whenToSeekCare: CRITICAL WARNING SIGNS: Severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding gums or nose, extreme lethargy/restlessness, or sudden breathlessness require immediate emergency hospitalization.

mythsAndFacts.myth: All dengue patients need platelet transfusions.
mythsAndFacts.fact: Platelet transfusions are indicated only when counts drop critically low or when there is active bleeding. Judicious fluid management is the primary cornerstone of dengue recovery.

faqs.question: Can I get dengue more than once?
faqs.answer: Yes. There are four distinct viral serotypes. Recovery provides lifelong immunity against that specific serotype, but only temporary cross-protection against others.

name: Malaria
tagline: Parasitic Infection: Cyclical Chills, Blood Smear Diagnostics & Treatment
summary: Malaria is a mosquito-borne illness caused by Plasmodium parasites, characterized by cyclical high fevers, rigors, and sweating.
whatIsIt: Malaria is an acute febrile illness caused by Plasmodium parasites (commonly Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium falciparum in India). It spreads through the bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. After entering the bloodstream, parasites multiply within the liver and subsequently invade and rupture red blood cells.
causes: Infection with Plasmodium parasites transmitted by night-biting Anopheles mosquitoes.
howItSpreads: Rarely through unscreened blood transfusion or contaminated needles
howItDoesNotSpread: Not contagious through casual contact, touch, or saliva
symptoms: Cyclical fever episodes with shaking chills (rigors)
High temperature followed by profuse sweating as fever breaks
Headache, muscle aches, and fatigue
Nausea, vomiting, and mild jaundice in severe cases
riskFactors: Warm humid regions, outdoor sleeping without mosquito nets, unmanaged stagnant puddles
testing: Peripheral blood smear examination (thick and thin films for parasite identification) and Rapid Diagnostic Tests (RDT for Pf/Pv antigens).
diagnosisOverview: Microscopic blood smear verification or antigen detection alongside clinical evaluation.
prevention: Insecticide-treated bed nets and window screens
Eliminating vector breeding habitats
Chemoprophylaxis for high-risk travelers
treatmentOverview: Antimalarial medications prescribed based on the specific Plasmodium species and regional drug sensitivity (e.g., Artemisinin-based combination therapies or Chloroquine/Primaquine under physician supervision).
whenToSeekCare: Immediate medical attention is required for recurring high fever with chills, or any signs of confusion, severe jaundice, or dark urine.

mythsAndFacts.myth: Malaria goes away on its own without medication.
mythsAndFacts.fact: Untreated malaria, especially P. falciparum, can progress to life-threatening cerebral complications or severe anemia.

faqs.question: Why does malaria require follow-up medication?
faqs.answer: For P. vivax, a 14-day course of Primaquine is often prescribed under physician supervision to eradicate dormant liver hypnozoites and prevent relapse.

name: Typhoid Fever
tagline: Enteric Bacterial Infection: Step-Ladder Fever, Food Safety & Care
summary: Typhoid is a bacterial infection caused by Salmonella Typhi, primarily transmitted through contaminated food or water.
whatIsIt: Typhoid fever is an enteric bacterial infection caused by Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi. In endemic regions, it is predominantly spread through ingestion of food or drinking water contaminated with fecal matter from an infected person or carrier. It produces prolonged 'step-ladder' rising fever, abdominal discomfort, and systemic toxicity.
causes: Ingestion of Salmonella Typhi bacteria through contaminated food, unboiled water, or poor hand hygiene.
howItSpreads: Fecal-oral route via contaminated food or water
Direct transmission from asymptomatic chronic carriers with poor hand hygiene
symptoms: Prolonged step-ladder fever that rises incrementally over several days
Headache, generalized weakness, and body ache
Abdominal pain, bloating, constipation (more common in adults) or diarrhea (in children)
Loss of appetite and coated tongue
Rose-colored spots on the chest or abdomen (in some cases)
riskFactors: Drinking untreated municipal or well water, street food with questionable hygiene, lack of sanitation
testing: Blood Culture (gold standard during 1st week), Widal test (serology, interpreted cautiously), Stool culture, Complete Blood Count (often shows leukopenia).
diagnosisOverview: Confirmed by isolating Salmonella Typhi from blood, bone marrow, or stool culture.
prevention: Typhoid Conjugate Vaccine (TCV): Highly effective single-dose immunization available at CareSphere
Drinking boiled, filtered, or sealed bottled water
Eating thoroughly cooked hot foods and peeling fresh fruits
Rigorous handwashing with soap before eating and after toilet use
treatmentOverview: Appropriate antibiotic therapy guided by culture sensitivity tests, along with adequate fluid intake, light nourishing diet, and fever management.
whenToSeekCare: Seek medical evaluation for fevers persisting beyond 3 days, especially accompanied by abdominal pain, severe headache, or gastrointestinal disturbances.

mythsAndFacts.myth: A single Widal test is always definitive proof of typhoid.
mythsAndFacts.fact: Widal tests can produce false positives due to prior infections or cross-reactions. Blood culture is the diagnostic standard.

faqs.question: Is there a vaccine for typhoid?
faqs.answer: Yes, Typhoid Conjugate Vaccines (TCV) provide robust, long-lasting immunity for children and adults.

name: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
tagline: Metabolic Health: Glycemic Control, HbA1c & Organ Protection
summary: Type 2 Diabetes is a chronic condition that impairs insulin sensitivity and glucose regulation. Proactive lifestyle modifications and medical management preserve long-term health.
whatIsIt: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus is a metabolic disorder characterized by persistent hyperglycemia (elevated blood glucose) resulting from insulin resistance combined with progressive beta-cell dysfunction in the pancreas. With thoughtful dietary habits, regular physical activity, and modern therapeutics, blood glucose can be safely controlled to prevent microvascular and macrovascular complications.
causes: Combination of genetic susceptibility, abdominal adiposity, sedentary lifestyle, and impaired insulin receptor signaling.
symptoms: Increased thirst (polydipsia) and dry mouth
Frequent urination (polyuria), especially at night
Increased hunger (polyphagia) despite eating
Unexplained fatigue and lethargy
Blurry vision and slow-healing cuts or sores
Tingling or numbness in the fingers or feet (neuropathy)
riskFactors: Overweight or higher visceral abdominal fat
Sedentary lifestyle and lack of aerobic exercise
Age above 35 years or history of gestational diabetes
testing: Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG), Postprandial Glucose (PPBS), Glycated Hemoglobin (HbA1c), Urine Microalbumin.
diagnosisOverview: Fasting blood sugar ≥ 126 mg/dL, 2-hour postprandial ≥ 200 mg/dL, or HbA1c ≥ 6.5% on two separate occasions.
prevention: Balanced diet rich in fiber, whole grains, and lean proteins with minimal refined sugars
At least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity weekly
Weight management and avoidance of smoking
Annual preventive health checkups after age 30
treatmentOverview: Multifaceted approach including nutritional counselling, regular exercise, oral anti-diabetic medications (e.g., Metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors), and insulin therapy when indicated.
whenToSeekCare: Consult a diabetologist for persistently elevated blood sugars, vision changes, foot sores that do not heal, or frequent urinary tract infections.

mythsAndFacts.myth: Eating sugar is the sole cause of diabetes.
mythsAndFacts.fact: Type 2 diabetes develops from a complex interplay of genetic predisposition, overall metabolic health, lifestyle, and insulin resistance.

faqs.question: What is a healthy target HbA1c?
faqs.answer: For most non-pregnant adults with diabetes, an HbA1c goal below 7.0% is recommended, though individual targets are personalized by your physician.

name: Bronchial Asthma
tagline: Airway Inflammation: Inhaler Technique, Triggers & Breathing Ease
summary: Asthma is a chronic condition causing reversible airway inflammation, bronchospasm, and episodic wheezing.
whatIsIt: Bronchial asthma is a chronic respiratory condition where the airways become inflamed, narrowed, and swollen, producing extra mucus. This leads to episodic breathing difficulties, chest tightness, wheezing, and coughing, often triggered by environmental allergens, cold air, or physical exertion.
causes: Airway hyper-reactivity caused by a combination of genetic atopy and environmental triggers such as pollen, dust mites, vehicular pollution, smoke, and viral upper respiratory infections.
symptoms: Wheezing (a musical whistling sound when exhaling)
Shortness of breath and difficulty catching breath
Chest tightness or pain
Chronic nighttime or early morning coughing
riskFactors: Family history of asthma or eczema (atopy)
Exposure to tobacco smoke, dust, industrial fumes, or frequent childhood respiratory infections
testing: Spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility testing, Peak Expiratory Flow Rate (PEFR) monitoring, and Chest X-Ray to exclude other causes.
diagnosisOverview: Clinical history of episodic symptoms confirmed by documented reversible airflow limitation on spirometry.
prevention: Identify and minimize exposure to known environmental triggers (dust, mold, pet dander)
Use protective dust masks in polluted or dusty conditions
Keep inhaler spacers clean and maintain annual influenza vaccines
treatmentOverview: Inhaled corticosteroids (controller inhalers) to reduce underlying inflammation, paired with short-acting beta-agonists (reliever inhalers) for acute symptom relief under medical supervision.
whenToSeekCare: Seek emergency medical help if wheezing does not respond to reliever inhaler, speech is limited to single words due to breathlessness, or lips turn bluish.

mythsAndFacts.myth: Inhalers are habit-forming and should be used as a last resort.
mythsAndFacts.fact: Inhaled medications deliver micro-doses directly to the lungs with minimal systemic absorption, making them much safer and more effective than oral tablets.

faqs.question: Can people with asthma exercise safely?
faqs.answer: Yes. Well-controlled asthma should not prevent regular sports or exercise. A preventive puff of reliever inhaler before exercise is often recommended.

name: High Blood Pressure (Hypertension)
tagline: The Silent Condition: Blood Pressure Monitoring, Diet & Heart Protection
summary: Hypertension is a chronic elevation of systemic arterial blood pressure. Early detection prevents heart attacks, strokes, and kidney disease.
whatIsIt: Hypertension is diagnosed when systemic blood pressure is consistently 140/90 mmHg or higher. Often called the 'silent killer' because it typically causes no overt symptoms in early stages, sustained high pressure gradually stiffens arteries and strains the heart muscle, kidneys, and brain.
causes: Primary (essential) hypertension develops gradually from age, arterial stiffening, excess sodium, and stress. Secondary hypertension stems from underlying kidney disease, sleep apnea, or endocrine conditions.
symptoms: Most commonly asymptomatic ('silent')
Occasional morning headaches or neck tightness
Dizziness or lightheadedness
Shortness of breath with moderate exertion
Nosebleeds (epistaxis) in very severe spikes
riskFactors: High dietary sodium, obesity, lack of physical activity, chronic stress, tobacco and alcohol use, age > 40
testing: Serial blood pressure recordings, 24-hour Ambulatory Blood Pressure Monitoring (ABPM), 12-lead ECG, Lipid Profile, Kidney Function Test.
diagnosisOverview: Confirmed by documented readings of ≥ 140/90 mmHg across at least two separate clinical visits.
prevention: DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) diet rich in vegetables, fruits, and potassium
Restricting dietary table salt to less than 5 grams per day
Regular brisk walking (30 minutes 5 days a week)
Smoking cessation and stress relaxation
treatmentOverview: Antihypertensive medications (e.g., ACE inhibitors, ARBs, Calcium Channel Blockers) prescribed according to cardiovascular risk, alongside lifestyle modifications.
whenToSeekCare: A blood pressure spike > 180/120 mmHg accompanied by chest pain, shortness of breath, blurry vision, or numbness represents a hypertensive emergency requiring immediate hospital care.

mythsAndFacts.myth: I feel completely fine, so my blood pressure must be normal.
mythsAndFacts.fact: High blood pressure rarely causes symptoms until organ damage has already started. Routine measurement is the only reliable way to know.

faqs.question: Can I stop blood pressure medicines once readings normalize?
faqs.answer: No. Blood pressure normalizes because the medicine is working. Any modification or reduction must be made under physician direction.
